content: The provided text contains detailed information about the interactions between ginger and various medications or substances, particularly focusing on their combined effects on anticoagulation. Indication-Specific Dosing for Ginger (African, Black, Cochin, and Combinations): 1. For motion sickness prevention: Administer 1–4 grams orally (PO) 5–4 hours before travel. Do not exceed 4 grams per day. 2. For general use: 170 mg PO three times daily (TID) or 255 mg PO twice daily (BID). Maximum daily dose: 4 grams. 3. For nausea/vomiting of pregnancy: 250 mg of ginger powder PO four times daily (QID). The dose may be increased up to 6 grams per day if necessary. Therapeutic Effects of Ginger: Ginger demonstrates antiemetic, carminative, stimulant, and anti-inflammatory properties. It is used for conditions such as dyspepsia, migraine headaches, morning sickness, motion sickness, chemotherapy-induced nausea, postoperative nausea/vomiting, osteoarthritis, respiratory infections, rheumatoid arthritis, and during SSRI tapering or discontinuation. Efficacy Evidence: Ginger has shown proven antiemetic efficacy in pregnancy-related nausea, postoperative nausea/vomiting, and vertigo. It is possibly ineffective for motion sickness. There is insufficient reliable data to evaluate its use in chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting, migraine headaches, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Drug and Herb Interactions with Ginger: 1. Increased Anticoagulation Risk: Ginger, when combined with certain medications or herbs, can enhance anticoagulant effects, potentially increasing the risk of bleeding. These include: Medications: Aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, celecoxib, ketorolac, indomethacin, meloxicam, bivalirudin, dabigatran, enoxaparin, heparin, dalteparin, fondaparinux, argatroban, alteplase, reteplase, tenecteplase, and protamine. Herbs and Supplements: Garlic, ginkgo biloba, feverfew, cinnamon, cordyceps, fennel, dong quai, devil’s claw, Panax ginseng, Siberian ginseng, agrimony, alfalfa, and anamu. Clinical Recommendation: Use caution and monitor closely when combining ginger with these agents. In some cases, therapy modification may be required. 2. Pharmacodynamic Synergism: Ginger may exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism with antiplatelet agents such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticlopidine, cilostazol, eptifibatide, and tirofiban. This interaction may prolong bleeding time. Clinical Recommendation: Use with caution due to conflicting evidence and unknown clinical significance. 3. Conflicting Effects on Anticoagulation: Ginger increases anticoagulation, while certain substances like mistletoe and nettle decrease it. The net effect of these interactions is unclear. Clinical Recommendation: Exercise caution and monitor closely. 4. Green Tea Interaction: Combining ginger with green tea may pose a risk due to the antiplatelet effects of both. Clinical Recommendation: Use caution when combining green tea with ginger or other herbs with anticoagulant properties. General Guidance: Ginger has a wide range of therapeutic applications but requires careful consideration of its interactions with anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, and other substances. Close monitoring is essential when ginger is used alongside medications or herbs that affect coagulation to prevent adverse effects such as prolonged bleeding.
